title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims “near-perfect accuracy in all tested scenarios,” while the reported results are far from near-perfect: e.g., Table 2 link-prediction accuracies are often about 40–60% and ROC-AUC values about 35–46%; Table 5 graph-classification ROC-AUC values are roughly 42–53%. The conclusion further claims that the method “completely solves” the two challenges and achieves “unprecedented and universal gains ... across all possible graph domains and tasks,” which is unsupported by experiments on a limited set of datasets and tasks.

The paper repeatedly claims faithful reasoning, reduction/elimination of hallucinations, and “reasoning faithfulness,” but reports no faithfulness, factuality, hallucination, grounding, calibration, or evidence-attribution metric. All reported outcomes are predictive metrics such as Accuracy, Recall, ROC-AUC, MSE, and R^2. Improved predictive scores alone do not establish that predictions are faithful or non-hallucinatory.

The text says “GLEM+RAG4GFM achieves 83.12% accuracy on node classification in the Computers dataset.” Table 2 reports 87.34 for GLEM+RAG4GFM on Computers node-classification accuracy, not 83.12. The incorrect number is repeated in the following paragraph.

Table 1 lists four Amazon/TAG datasets as Books-Children, Books-History, Ele-Computers, and Ele-Photo. Table 2 instead reports Computers, History, Fitness, and Photo. “Fitness” is not listed anywhere in Table 1 or the dataset description, and the paper never maps it to a dataset. Thus a full column of principal results cannot be linked to a declared dataset.

Table 3 reports AnyGraph-based RAG4GFM results of 63.45 Accuracy and 64.12 ROC-AUC for “History (Link Pred.).” These are exactly the node-classification History values for AnyGraph+RAG4GFM in Table 2 (63.45 and 64.12). Table 2's actual History link-prediction values for AnyGraph+RAG4GFM are 41.74 Accuracy and 43.26 ROC-AUC. Thus Table 3 mislabels copied node-classification results as link-prediction results.

The claimed full-model History link-prediction result is 63.5 Accuracy and 64.1 AUC. These round to the History node-classification values 63.45 and 64.12 in Table 2, not the History link-prediction values 41.74 and 43.26. Appendix C.2 independently reports 41.74 as the K=3 History link-prediction score, confirming that the ablation heading or its data are wrong.

The method defines A' = A + sum_i alpha_i^T A_i, directly adding adjacency matrices from the query graph and retrieved graphs. Retrieved graphs generally have different numbers of nodes and no shared node ordering or node correspondence, so their adjacency matrices have incompatible dimensions and cannot be added. No alignment, graph matching, padding convention, or node-mapping function is defined. This makes the central topology-fusion operation mathematically undefined for the stated graph-retrieval setting.

Equation (8) calls h'_v^G an enhanced “target graph feature,” but it remains indexed by node v and combines only h_v; it neither defines the node set over which it operates nor aggregates retrieved graph features. Equation (9) computes h_v · (h_g^q + h_g^i), although h_g in Equation (2) is a concatenation of node, edge, and 3-dimensional graph statistics, whereas h_v is an unspecified node feature. Their dimensions are generally incompatible without a projection, which is not provided. The SOFTMAX normalization axis is also unspecified.

The reciprocal-rank-fusion score is not well defined. Equation (3) sums over x in F(h_q,C), but Equation (4) defines F as a set of feature representations rather than a set of retrieved candidates or ranked lists. rank_x^k(C) is described as a corpus rank but no query-dependent ranking function is specified. In the graph-level branch Equation (4) uses h_q(G), which is never defined; the graph encoding defined earlier is h_g(G). Consequently the stated equations do not specify an implementable retrieval score.

The paper states that Laplacian positional encoding plus degrees is “invariant to node permutations and graph isomorphism.” Raw Laplacian eigenvectors have sign ambiguity, and eigenspaces with repeated eigenvalues have arbitrary rotations/basis choices. Without sign handling, eigenspace-invariant processing, or a canonicalization procedure, the stated LapPE representation is not generally invariant in the claimed sense.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract; Section 3.1 Hierarchical Index Construction; Appendix A.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract and Section 3.1 claim “constant-time retrieval and fusion for all graph sizes” and later claim O(log N) end-to-end retrieval and fusion. Appendix A directly contradicts this: it gives per-query complexity O(log N + k|V|^2) for dense graphs or O(log N + k|E|) for sparse graphs. Fusion therefore grows with retrieved graph size/edge count and is neither constant-time nor logarithmic in all graph sizes and densities.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A.1, Multi-level Graph Indexing complexity
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed O(N log N) indexing complexity omits the cost of computing Laplacian positional encodings for both the original graph and its line graph. Exact Laplacian eigendecomposition is substantially more expensive than O(N log N) in general, and construction/eigendecomposition of a line graph can itself be very costly for high-degree graphs. No approximate eigensolver, number of eigenvectors, or complexity assumptions are supplied, so the stated end-to-end indexing complexity is not justified.

The paper never specifies what data populate the retrieval index relative to train/validation/test splits. This is critical because it indexes raw graph topology and then retrieves/fuses subgraphs for node and link prediction. If the full graph, including held-out test edges or test-neighborhood structure, is indexed, link-prediction evaluation can leak test information. The paper also does not state whether labels, target nodes, or test graph instances are excluded from retrieval. Without this protocol the reported evaluation cannot be assessed for leakage or reproduced.

Table 3 compares an AnyGraph-based RAG4GFM system against few-shot prompting, CoT, IR-augmented CoT, prototypical networks, GNNSafe, VanillaRAG, GraphRAG, and G-Retriever, but does not identify a common backbone, input representation, retrieval corpus, training budget, prompt/model, or tuning protocol for these heterogeneous methods. Several listed methods are not interchangeable GFM wrappers. Therefore the table does not establish the claimed superiority of the proposed method under a controlled comparison.

Table 4 compares GraphLoRA “training time” to RAG4GFM time but does not state whether RAG4GFM time includes construction of text embeddings, LapPE, line-graph encodings, HNSW indices, task classification, or retrieval-corpus refreshes. It also gives only target accuracy rather than matched evaluation protocols and does not state the task/split corresponding to each target. Comparing inference-side retrieval time excluding index construction to fine-tuning wall-clock time is not a valid demonstration of a 7x updating advantage.

The paper claims to demonstrate efficient knowledge updating, but it evaluates static benchmark datasets and gives no experiment in which graph knowledge changes over time, no update latency, no index-refresh cost, and no performance before/after an update. A comparison against fine-tuning runtime alone does not demonstrate knowledge-update performance or robustness to evolving graphs.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 1, Appendix C.1 Table 6 description, and Table 5/6 heading
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: WN18 is designated “LC” (link classification) in Table 1 and the supplementary table header says “WN18Dataset (Link Class.),” but the Appendix C.1 prose calls the same evaluation “link prediction (WN18)” and says the method improves results on “link prediction.” These are distinct tasks with different negative sampling and split protocols; the paper never resolves which task was actually evaluated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 1 and Appendix B.1, QM7bDataset citation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 1 cites QM7bDataset only as [53], and Appendix B.1 cites it as “[53, 64].” Reference [53] is Blum and Reymond's paper on the GDB-13 chemical universe database, not the QM7/QM7b molecular-property benchmark. Reference [64] is the relevant Rupp et al. molecular atomization-energy work. Attribution of QM7b to [53] is erroneous and should be corrected.

The statement that using TAG “prevent[s] potential data leakage from GFM pre-training” is not established. Publication in a recent benchmark does not show that its underlying Amazon graph/text content was absent from the pretraining corpora of every evaluated GFM or LLM. No pretraining-corpus audit, temporal cutoff, contamination test, or model-specific evidence is provided.
